common_meaning: In fact; as things really are, often in contrast to what was expected, assumed or said before.
example: I thought the shop closed at six, but it actually closes at eight.
rrgm_bridge: Actually marks a correction arriving: the speaker sets a checked state of affairs against an earlier belief and lets the checked one stand.
invariant_mi: Asserts that what follows is the real case, set against an expectation or earlier claim that it overrides.

domain_entries.LIN: A stance adverb: it signals contrast with an assumption and is often used to soften a correction or disagreement in conversation.
domain_entries.COG: Marks belief revision in speech: the prior expectation is named or implied, and the update is offered as the outcome of a check.

count_condition: There is an earlier expectation, claim or assumption, stated or implied, that the actually-clause contradicts or refines.
transfer_boundary: Saying "actually" does not make a claim checked; it signals the speaker's confidence in the correction, which still needs its own evidence. As a filler ("actually, yeah") it carries little more than emphasis.

common_meaning: Causing great surprise or wonder; informally, very good.
example: The view from the top was amazing.
rrgm_bridge: Amazing marks an experience that outran expectation by a wide margin.
invariant_mi: Exceeding expectation so far as to cause wonder.

domain_entries.AFF: Surprise and delight at something beyond what was anticipated. Parity line: whether a given system feels amazement is [UNK] under the Symmetry Rule. Provisional domain.
domain_entries.LIN: Heavily used as general praise, which has weakened its force.

count_condition: An experience or thing that exceeds what the speaker expected.
transfer_boundary: Calling something amazing reports the speaker's reaction, not a measured quality. Overuse makes it closer to "good".

common_meaning: (Adjective) Respected and impressive, of high standing.
example: The award was presented before an august audience of scientists.
rrgm_bridge: August gives standing to a body or person by age, rank or achievement.
invariant_mi: Marked by dignity and high regard.

domain_entries.REL: Signals respect for an institution's or person's standing.
domain_entries.LIN: Formal register; unrelated in use to the month August (a proper noun), though both come from the Roman title Augustus.

count_condition: A person, body or occasion regarded as dignified and eminent.
transfer_boundary: Standing is not correctness: an august body can still be wrong.

common_meaning: Further forward in space or time; in front; also in a leading position.
example: The road ahead is closed; our team is two points ahead.
rrgm_bridge: Ahead points along the direction of travel, to what has not been reached yet.
invariant_mi: In front, in the direction of motion or in the future.

domain_entries.REL: "Getting ahead" names gaining advantage over others.

count_condition: A position further along a path, sequence or ranking.
transfer_boundary: Being ahead now is not winning; the lead can change.

common_meaning: A donkey; also (vulgar) the buttocks; also (vulgar, insult) a foolish or unpleasant person.
example: The farmer led the ass to market; don't be an ass.
rrgm_bridge: Ass starts as the name of a working animal and is turned into both a body word and an insult.
invariant_mi: A donkey, or a vulgar word for the buttocks or for a fool.

domain_entries.BIO: The donkey, Equus asinus, a domesticated working animal.
domain_entries.LIN: Vulgar in the body sense; American "ass" and British "arse" overlap.
domain_entries.PEJ: As an insult, calls a person stupid or obnoxious; the mechanism borrows the donkey's old reputation for stubborn stupidity.

count_condition: A donkey, the buttocks, or a person being insulted.
transfer_boundary: The animal sense is neutral; the other senses are vulgar or insulting and depend on register.

common_meaning: Completely; totally; also used as strong agreement.
rrgm_bridge: Absolutely removes every qualification from what it modifies.
invariant_mi: Without any limit, condition or exception.

domain_entries.FOR: An absolute claim allows no exceptions, so one counter-case breaks it.

count_condition: A statement marked as unqualified, or strong agreement.
transfer_boundary: "Absolutely" as agreement is emphasis, not evidence. Absolute claims are the easiest to refute.

common_meaning: To have the same opinion; to consent to something; to match or be consistent.
example: We agree on the plan; the figures don't agree.
rrgm_bridge: To agree is to arrive at the same position from two sides, whether in view, consent or fit.
invariant_mi: To share a view, consent, or correspond.

domain_entries.REL: Agreement can be genuine, or given under pressure; consent that cannot be refused is not free.
domain_entries.FOR: Two results agree when they match within the expected error.

count_condition: Two parties sharing a view or consent, or two things that match.
transfer_boundary: Agreement under pressure tells you about the pressure. Agreeing to a plan is not agreeing with every part of it.

common_meaning: Any longer; at present (in some dialects, in positive sentences too).
rrgm_bridge: Anymore marks a state that has ended, set against when it held.

domain_entries.LIN: Mostly used with negatives; "positive anymore" ("anymore, we eat late") is regional.

count_condition: A former state contrasted with now.
transfer_boundary: Something not done anymore was once done; the word implies a past.
